title: How plants make their food
source: hand-written sample (stands in for model output until the fine-tuned model exists)
passage: All living things need food. Animals eat plants or other animals, but green plants make their own food. This process is called photosynthesis. It happens mainly in the leaves. Leaves contain a green pigment called chlorophyll, which traps the energy of sunlight. The energy itself is not food; the plant uses it to build food from simpler materials. Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air through tiny pores on the underside of their leaves, called stomata. Water is absorbed by the roots from the soil and carried up the stem to the leaves. Minerals also come from the soil, but they are not the plant's food; they help the plant stay healthy. Inside the leaf, the trapped energy is used to join carbon dioxide and water to make a sugar called glucose. Oxygen is released into the air as a by-product. Extra glucose is changed into starch and stored in different parts of the plant, such as roots, stems and seeds. This is why we can test a leaf for starch to find out whether it has been making food. Without photosynthesis there would be no food for animals and very little oxygen in the air. Almost every food chain on Earth begins with a green plant capturing the energy of the Sun.
summary: Green plants make their own food by photosynthesis, mostly in their leaves. Chlorophyll traps sunlight energy. The plant uses this energy to join carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil into glucose, and gives out oxygen. Extra glucose is stored as starch. Almost all food chains start with this process.

misconceptions.text: Plants get their food ready-made from the soil
misconceptions.fix: Soil gives water and minerals, but minerals only keep the plant healthy. The food itself (glucose) is made inside the leaf.

misconceptions.text: Plants eat like animals do, taking food in through their roots
misconceptions.fix: Roots take in water and minerals, not food. Plants are different from animals: they build their food themselves.

misconceptions.text: Fertiliser or minerals are the plant's food
misconceptions.fix: Fertiliser adds minerals, which help the plant stay healthy. They are not food; the plant still has to make glucose by photosynthesis.

misconceptions.text: Sunlight itself is the plant's food
misconceptions.fix: Sunlight is energy, not food. The plant uses that energy to build food (glucose) from carbon dioxide and water.

misconceptions.text: Sunlight only keeps the plant warm
misconceptions.fix: Light matters because chlorophyll traps its energy for making food. Warmth alone cannot make food.

misconceptions.text: Chlorophyll is just colour and does no work
misconceptions.fix: Chlorophyll is green, but its job is to trap the energy of sunlight. Without it the leaf cannot make food.

concepts.name: Raw materials: carbon dioxide and water

misconceptions.text: Plants take in oxygen, not carbon dioxide, to make food
misconceptions.fix: For photosynthesis plants take in carbon dioxide through the stomata. Oxygen is what they give out.

misconceptions.text: Water enters the plant mainly through the leaves
misconceptions.fix: Water is absorbed by the roots from the soil and carried up the stem to the leaves.

misconceptions.text: The soil is used up to build the plant's body
misconceptions.fix: The plant's food and body are built mostly from carbon dioxide from the air and water. Soil only supplies water and a small amount of minerals.

misconceptions.text: Photosynthesis is just the way plants breathe
misconceptions.fix: Photosynthesis is how plants make food. Giving out oxygen is a by-product, not the purpose.

misconceptions.text: Plants make only oxygen, not food
misconceptions.fix: The main product is glucose, the plant's food. Oxygen is released as a by-product.

misconceptions.text: Food is made in the roots and stored in the leaves
misconceptions.fix: Food is made in the leaves. Extra glucose is changed to starch and stored in roots, stems and seeds.

questions.stem: Where does a green plant's food come from?

options.text: It is taken ready-made from the soil
The plant makes it itself
The roots eat it, like an animal eats
It comes from the fertiliser farmers add

questions.explanation: Green plants make their own food by photosynthesis. Animals cannot do this, so they eat plants or other animals.

questions.stem: A farmer adds lots of mineral fertiliser to a field, but keeps the plants in a dark shed. What happens to their food supply?

options.text: Plenty of food, because the fertiliser is their food
Plenty of food, because the roots can eat from the rich soil
Plenty of food, because soil food is already there
They cannot make food, so they start to starve

questions.explanation: Minerals keep a plant healthy but are not food. In the dark the plant cannot make food, however rich the soil is.

questions.stem: What do minerals from the soil do for a plant?

options.text: They are the plant's main food
They help the plant stay healthy
They are food the roots swallow
They are ready-made food stored in soil

questions.explanation: The passage says minerals are not the plant's food; they help the plant stay healthy.

questions.stem: What does chlorophyll do in a leaf?

options.text: It traps the energy of sunlight
It only makes the leaf look green
It keeps the leaf warm in the sun
It stores sunlight as the plant's food

questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is a green pigment that traps sunlight energy. The plant then uses that energy to make food.

questions.stem: Two identical plants are kept equally warm. One gets sunlight, the other is kept in a warm dark cupboard. Which one can make food?

options.text: Both, because warmth is what plants need from the Sun
Only the one in sunlight, because its chlorophyll can trap light energy
Both, because green colour is all a leaf needs
Only the one in sunlight, because it is eating the light

questions.explanation: Warmth is the same for both plants, so it is not the difference. Only the plant in light can trap light energy and use it to make food.

questions.stem: Is sunlight itself the plant's food?

options.text: Yes, plants feed on sunlight
No, sunlight just warms the plant up
No, it gives energy that the plant uses to build food
No, only the green colour matters

questions.explanation: The passage says the energy itself is not food; the plant uses it to build food from simpler materials.

questions.stem: Which two raw materials does a plant join together to make glucose?

options.text: Oxygen and water
Carbon dioxide and water
Soil and water
Carbon dioxide and rainwater soaked up by the leaves

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide comes from the air through the stomata, and water comes from the soil through the roots.

questions.stem: A big tree grows from a tiny seed, yet the soil around it hardly gets less. Where did most of the tree's material come from?

options.text: From the soil, slowly used up over the years
From oxygen the leaves breathed in
From carbon dioxide in the air, joined with water
From rainwater the leaves soaked up

questions.explanation: The plant builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water, and uses it to grow. The soil supplies only water and a little mineral matter.

questions.stem: How does water reach the leaves?

options.text: The leaves soak it up from rain and dew
Roots absorb it from the soil and the stem carries it up
The stomata take it in along with oxygen
It comes from soil the plant uses up

questions.explanation: Water is absorbed by the roots from the soil and carried up the stem to the leaves.

questions.stem: What does a leaf make during photosynthesis?

options.text: Only oxygen for us to breathe
Nothing; photosynthesis is just how leaves breathe
Glucose, with oxygen given out as a by-product
Nothing; food is made in the roots and sent up

questions.explanation: The leaf makes glucose, the plant's food. Oxygen is released into the air as a by-product.

questions.stem: A student tests a potato (a swollen underground stem) and finds lots of starch. How did the starch get there?

options.text: Leaves made glucose; the extra was changed to starch and stored in the potato
The potato made it underground and will send it up to the leaves
It cannot be from photosynthesis, because plants only make oxygen
The potato breathes in starch from the soil

questions.explanation: Glucose is made in the leaves. Extra glucose is changed into starch and stored in roots, stems and seeds.

questions.stem: A leaf is kept in the dark for two days and then tested. It shows no starch. What does this tell us?

options.text: The leaf stopped breathing, so it lost its starch
Starch is only stored in roots, never in leaves
Nothing, because leaves make only oxygen anyway
Without light it could not make new food, and used up what it had

questions.explanation: Testing for starch tells us whether a leaf has been making food. In the dark there is no photosynthesis, so no new starch is made.
